Entrepreneurship theory explains how opportunities are recognised, evaluated and created, but it models every stage of that process as exclusively human. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now participates in all three stages: founders use large language models as co-ideators that generate opportunity candidates and as drafting partners that develop them, while investors use the same class of models to screen founders' submissions. This conceptual paper integrates opportunity theory (discovery, creation and effectuation) with the emerging empirical evidence on generative AI and ideation, creativity, evaluation and entrepreneurial performance. It argues that the co-ideator changes the opportunity process in four ways: it expands each founder's supply of candidates while compressing ideation skill gaps; it correlates opportunity pools across founders who draw on shared models, creating a homogenisation risk at market level; it raises the returns to prior knowledge, which governs selection among abundant machine-generated candidates; and it migrates durable advantage from generating opportunities to selecting, combining and enacting them. These claims are stated as seven formal propositions with boundary conditions, including the "jagged opportunity frontier" and the evaluation asymmetries produced by narrative AI explanations, with implications for founders, investors and educators, and a research agenda.

AIM: To assess a comprehensive model linking servant leadership, health-promoting leadership, workplace social climate, psychosocial safety climate, work conditions and healthcare workers' wellbeing. DESIGN: A cross-sectional survey design. METHODS: A total of 1563 healthcare workers completed a survey between 2024 and 2025. Structural equation modelling was employed to test the hypothesised relationships. RESULTS: Servant leadership, health-promoting leadership and workplace social climate were positively associated with healthcare workers' perceptions of psychosocial safety climate. Higher levels of psychosocial safety climate were linked to lower cognitive job demands and greater job resources, including job control, supervisor support and colleague support. These work conditions were associated with lower psychological strain and turnover intention, as well as higher job satisfaction and work engagement. Unexpectedly, cognitive job demands were positively related to work engagement, suggesting that cognitively challenging work may be perceived as meaningful and motivating in healthcare settings. CONCLUSIONS: Supportive leadership and a positive workplace social climate are important correlates of psychosocial safety climate, which was associated with healthier work conditions and better wellbeing among healthcare workers. In addition, the findings suggest that certain job demands may play a motivational as well as a straining role in healthcare contexts. IMPLICATIONS: Strengthening leadership practices and cultivating a supportive workplace social climate help healthcare organisations foster psychosocial safety climate and improve work conditions for healthcare workers. Enhancing these conditions supports healthcare workers' wellbeing and is associated with more sustainable healthcare workplaces. REPORTING METHOD: The STROBE checklist. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No patient or public contribution.

General-purpose conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for health-related questions, including questions relevant to cancer care, although breast-cancer-specific prevalence and behavioural effects remain poorly characterised. Most evaluations ask whether an AI answer is accurate. That is necessary but incomplete. Clinically consequential effects may arise when a fluent, apparently personalised exchange changes a treatment preference, delays contact with the clinical team, reinforces reassurance-seeking, validates non-adherence, or converts population guidance into an individual-sounding instruction. We conceptualise this as a parallel pathway: an AI-mediated sequence of questions, answers and actions that is usually invisible to the treating team, absent from the medical record and unattached to professional responsibility, yet capable of re-entering formal care through its downstream consequences. We distinguish model error from pathway error and propose traceability, reversibility, and returnability to accountable care as safety properties beyond answer accuracy. Across four clinical domains, we propose distinct pathway failure modes: premature preference closure in surgical decision-making; escalation closure during treatment toxicity; repetitive reassurance-seeking and over-reliance in psycho-oncology; and loss of conditionality in perioperative recovery and lifestyle advice. These are hypothesis-generating mechanisms rather than empirically established dominant patterns. We propose a five-step clinical response - ASK, RECONSTRUCT, CLASSIFY, CHECK and RETURN - based on non-judgemental inquiry, proportionate documentation and explicit return-to-care boundaries. Regulation can govern products and deployed systems, but it cannot by itself reveal patient-initiated consumer AI use. Clinical services therefore need governance for the pathway as well as for the technology.

documents.abstract: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) lowers the threshold for producing work, not necessarily for learning. This study examines how an instructor kept an interdisciplinary AI course teachable for first-year art students, where that effort reached its limits, and how the instructor interpreted students' engagement with AI tools. Methods The study is a longitudinal practitioner self-study of a 12-week course taught in autumn 2025 at a higher vocational college in northwestern China. The data are the instructor's own reflective journals: structured entries written during the semester for Weeks 1–7 and retrospective accounts of Weeks 8–12 written after the semester ended. The two strata are reported separately. Reflexive thematic analysis produced 40 evidence anchors, five themes, one cross-cutting thread, and one central organizing theme, with a full audit trail. Results The instructor's repairs (translating content into everyday and discipline-specific tasks, working around broken or restricted lab equipment, and demonstrating on the teacher's computer) kept the course running. However, as content moved toward frontier tools that required paid accounts, computing resources, and prior AI experience, teaching drifted toward demonstration (“the more cutting-edge something is, the more it can only be demonstrated”). Across the semester the instructor recorded a recurring pattern, here termed a teacher-perceived low-threshold illusion , in which students appeared, in the instructor's account, to treat seeing, bookmarking, or one-click generation as equivalent to being able to do. The instructor associated this pattern with three co-occurring conditions: natural-language prompting and one-click generation, demonstration-only teaching, and a final assessment that students could complete without having attended. Participation could be high while, in the instructor's judgement, students gained little. Conclusion Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in AI teaching is bounded. Keeping an AI course running did not by itself make learning visible: the journals record a tension between engagement, product completion, and evidence of learning, not an established failure of learning. In-course repair reached limits shaped by access conditions and an inherited assessment format, and reconstruction of the course took place at the scale of the semester. We present pedagogical resilience reconstruction as an emerging construct for multi-case testing.

This study investigates the relationship between creative learning videos and learning motivation among Generation Z students in the context of Islamic history education. Using a quantitative approach with correlational design, this research involved 30 students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using two main instruments: the Creative Learning Video Usage Questionnaire (CLVUQ) and Learning Motivation Scale (LMS), both demonstrating high reliability with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.906 and 0.942, respectively. The findings reveal a weak positive correlation (R = 0.340) between creative learning video usage and learning motivation, with an explanatory power of 11.6% (R Square = 0.116). A notably high acceptance rate of creative learning videos was reflected by 93.33% of respondents providing positive responses, with an average satisfaction score of 4.37 (SD = 0.62). Further analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation emerged as the most responsive dimension, with an average score of 4.12, compared to extrinsic motivation (3.89) and self-efficacy (4.01). These findings underscore the importance of integrating traditional and modern learning approaches in Islamic history education while emphasizing the need to consider contextual factors such as social, cultural, and institutional aspects in developing technology-based learning strategies. Despite certain methodological limitations, this research provides meaningful empirical foundations for developing more effective learning strategies in the digital era, particularly in the context of Islamic history education for Generation Z.

This study examined perceived influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on computational skills and independent reasoning among pre-service teachers in College of Education, Akwanga, Nasarawa State. Five research questions and three hypotheses guided the study. Descriptive survey design was adopted. Population was 125 NCE mathematics pre-service teachers, sample was 100 (62 males, 38 females) selected by simple random sampling. Instrument was Artificial Intelligence on Computational Skills and Mathematical Reasoning among Pre-Service Teachers (AI-CSMRPT) with reliability of 0.82 Cronbach Alpha. Mean and SD answered research questions, one-way ANOVA and one-sample t-test tested hypotheses at 0.05. Findings revealed AI significantly influences computational skills (Grand M=3.09) by improving speed (M=3.24) and accuracy (M=3.18). Both male (M=3.18) and female (M=2.95) agreed, but significant gender difference existed (F=4.67 > 3.94). AI also influences independent reasoning (Grand M=2.90), with reliance on AI before attempting problems (M=3.16) highest. Both genders agreed (M=2.98 male, M=2.77 female) with significant difference (F=4.12 > 3.94). No significant difference between influence on computational skills (M=3.09) and independent reasoning (M=2.90), p=0.47. Study concluded AI enhances computation but creates alternative cognition that reduces independent effort if unguided. Responsible and ethical use of AI as supplement, gender-sensitive training, and institutional guidelines were recommended.

documents.abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

Abstract The inference of physical laws has traditionally relied on human intuition, analytical reasoning, and experimental observation. However, modern physics research is increasingly constrained by challenges such as high specialization, fragmented workflows, and limited computational resources, which impede scientific progress. To address these issues, we introduce PhysAgent , a novel multi-agent system powered by large language models (LLMs), designed to execute end-to-end scientific workflows—from hypothesis generation and computational modeling to data analysis and reporting. PhysAgent’s innovation lies in its specialized agent collaboration: a Mentor Agent guides scientific reasoning through Socratic questioning, a Student Agent handles technical execution (e.g., code implementation, DFT calculations), and a Leader Agent dynamically optimizes task scheduling and resource allocation. Integrating domain-specific tools like first-principles simulations (e.g., Quantum ESPRESSO, VASP), PhysAgent aims to improve reproducibility while maintaining human-in-the-loop refinement. We demonstrate PhysAgent as a proof-of-concept framework for recovering known physical relations from controlled data, including Kepler-law recovery from orbital trajectories and Newton-law recovery from force-motion data. Furthermore, it extends to ab initio materials modeling, automating electronic structure workflows (e.g., GaAs band-structure and density-of-states calculations). In addition, PhysAgent simulates complex real-world phenomena, such as raindrop flow on train windows. By harmonizing LLM-driven planning with domain-specific tools, PhysAgent provides a reproducible multi-agent workflow for physics data analysis and simulation. We provide a demonstration video of PhysAgent to illustrate its workflow and capabilities: https://b23.tv/emOilkC.

documents.abstract: Abstract Digital games are present in the daily life of an increasing number of users, regardless of age, gender, or any other social or demographic characteristics. Their importance has evolved from their original purpose for entertainment to a tool used in education as well as for acquiring or improving an ever-widening range of certain skills and knowledge. The use of digital games in various aspects of life is expanding every day. The main goal of our research is a systematized presentation of the characteristics of kinesthetic digital games which, in conjunction with virtual reality and artificial intelligence elements, provide users with a far more realistic game experience. The research was conducted through a systematic review of literature from appropriate and relevant e-repositories. The paper presents the results of the research, as well as certain conclusions derived from the results obtained. Kinesthetic digital games offer numerous advantages such as promoting physical activity, improving cognitive skills, improving social interaction and availability to a wide range of individuals. However, there are some shortcomings, including potential security risks, limited physical activity, limited possibilities of social interaction and injury from excessive use. Despite these shortcomings, kinesthetic digital games remain a popular and effective way to involve physical activity and entertainment into a daily routine. It is necessary to maintain a balance between kinesthetic digital games and other forms of physical activity with careful tracking of instructions and use appropriate precautions to maximize the advantages of these games. The prospects for further development of kinesthetic digital games are promising. As technology continues to progress, we can expect more innovative and interactive games that will provide players more impressive and useful experience. The paper represents an initial step in research into the possibilities and methods of applying kinesthetic digital games in teaching at higher education institutions.

Objective To investigate the physiological and thermal effects of a passive assistive suit during repetitive work in a hot environment. Methods Ten healthy adult males performed a repetitive stepping task in a hot environment (35°C, 50% relative humidity) under a control condition (CON) and an assistive-suit condition (EXO). Nine participants completed both conditions and were included in the analyses. Rectal temperature (T re ), mean skin temperature (T sk ), heart rate (HR), oxygen uptake ( V ˙ O 2 ) , lower-limb rating of perceived exertion (RPE), and the number of step ascents were assessed. HR was normalized to the resting value, defined as 100% (%HR). Results The number of step ascents was significantly higher in EXO during the later sets (p < 0.05). No significant between-condition difference was observed in ΔT re (EXO, 1.08°C ± 0.30°C; CON, 1.06°C ± 0.30°C; p = 0.870, Cohen's d = 0.06). EXO led to a significantly higher increase in T sk than CON (2.11°C ± 0.43°C vs. 1.76°C ± 0.35°C; p = 0.024, Cohen's d = 0.88). Lower-limb RPE was significantly lower in the EXO from 11 min after exercise onset (p < 0.05). No significant effects of the conditions were observed for %HR (p = 0.646) and V ˙ O 2 (p = 0.133). Conclusion Under the present experimental conditions, passive assistive suit use improved task performance and reduced perceived lower-limb exertion without a detectable increase in core thermal strain.

Chest radiography is the most widely performed imaging examination worldwide and serves as a first-line test across emergency, inpatient and outpatient care. Its interpretation is nevertheless demanding, and diagnostic errors, including missed pneumonia, pulmonary nodules and pleural effusions, are frequent even among experienced readers [1]. Rising imaging volumes and radiologist workforce constraints have accelerated interest in artificial intelligence (AI) decision support, and by 2022 about 190 radiologic AI programs had received approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration, with approvals increasing each year [2,3]. Controlled reader studies show that AI assistance can improve performance when the algorithm is accurate. In a retrospective multireader multicase study, the macro-averaged area under the curve (AUC) of radiologists across 127 chest radiograph findings rose from 0.713 unaided to 0.808 with AI assistance [4]. Another reader study reported higher AUROCs for pneumothorax (0.885 to 0.969) and nodules (0.724 to 0.752), together with a roughly 10% reduction in reporting time [5]. These results have supported the view that AI will help readers by default. AI output is, however, never perfectly accurate. A review of 503 algorithm studies, cited in recent human-factors work in radiology, reported pooled sensitivity of 0.87 and specificity of 0.89 for chest radiograph abnormalities, implying that about 13 of 100 abnormal examinations and 11 of 100 normal examinations would receive an erroneous output [6]. The clinical value of AI therefore depends not only on algorithm accuracy but also on how readers respond when the algorithm is wrong.

documents.abstract: This study examines the extent to which generative artificial intelligence aligns with human experts in the visual assessment of urban open spaces. Site quality is addressed across five dimensions: spatial accessibility and organization; usage and social function; environmental quality and comfort; safety and inclusivity; and perceptual and aesthetic quality. The same images, indicators, and five-point scale regarding three heavily used public open spaces in Rize city center were evaluated by 20 architects and landscape architects, as well as by ChatGPT and Gemini. The comparison revealed that the level of agreement between the AI and the experts varied depending on the specific site and quality dimension. While alignment was high regarding features that are directly observable—both physically and visually—differences became more pronounced regarding perceptual and aesthetic qualities. The findings suggest that AI can serve as a complementary tool to support visual assessment rather than a replacement for human expertise.

The emergence of artificial intelligence in primary education is changing the way teaching materials are structured, information is acquired, and learning decisions are made. These changes require a reconsideration of the teacher's position, particularly when system recommendations begin to influence assessments of children's needs and abilities. This article aims to redefine the role of primary school teachers through the relationship between pedagogical agency, knowledge authority, and educational ethics. The review employs a critical narrative literature approach to 19 selected publications from 2021–2026, encompassing empirical research, research reviews, conceptual articles, and policy documents that provide open access or official download facilities. The literature is reviewed based on educational context, type of evidence, conceptual contributions, and limitations of its application to primary schools. The synthesis shows that the benefits of AI depend on learning objectives, professional judgment capacity, and institutional support. Teacher agency requires the authority to review, modify, and reject system recommendations. Knowledge authority rests on the ability to explain the basis for a claim and guide the examination of evidence. Educational ethics need to be embodied in data protection, equitable access, child engagement, and the sharing of responsibilities. The article proposes the role of teachers as learning designers, knowledge assessors, relational facilitators, and advocates for children's interests. This reconceptualization requires case-based professional development and school governance that does not center all technological risks on teachers.

documents.abstract: Embodied foundation models have expanded robot capabilities, but autonomous execution does not automatically provide autonomous improvement. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) concerns retained changes that can influence subsequent improvement, including the stronger case in which an agent revises the procedures that generate and evaluate future updates. This survey connects large-model learning and reasoning, agent memory and skills, and RSI theory. We compare general agent harnesses with embodied harnesses and organize the literature along four axes: improvement targets, update mechanisms, decision authority and evidence conditions. The method review covers reflection and knowledge revision, executable programs and harness evolution, adaptive experience acquisition, parameter learning, world-model revision, and cross-layer selection and meta-improvement. We analyze how large models guide interventions across these components and distinguish execution correction, persistent capability improvement and revision of the improver. Long-horizon tasks and physical priors are examined as complementary considerations for memory, execution, world modeling and evaluation within this broader framework. We compare representative methods and review benchmarks, datasets, development partitions and resource accounting. Existing evidence supports several forms of retained improvement, while comparable evidence for improved improvement procedures remains limited. Open problems include causal failure attribution, reliable feedback, safe inheritance, competence preservation, model validity, transferable improvers and principled stopping decisions.

Interactive technology is increasingly built for speed, and generative AI now answers before a question is fully formed. Yet the capacity to pause, interpret and decide for oneself is central to wellbeing, learning and meaningful use. HCI has named paradigms for sensing emotion, changing behavior, calming attention and tracking the self. However, none of them takes human reflection, and the slowing down it requires, as its organizing aim. This article defines that paradigm, reflective computing, and derives it from what thirty years of designs lack. We analyzed 134 interactive systems from 17 ACM venues (1996-2026) in two phases. First, an abductive gap analysis read every system against reflection theory, and seven recurring gaps defined seven dimensions, namely tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness and ethical non-extraction. Second, two independent coders scored every system with a codebook (Krippendorff's alpha 0.67 to 0.84 for five dimensions; ICC 0.82 for the overall score). The system sets the pace in 51 designs, 74 support only momentary use, only 12 scaffold reflection beyond description, and 56 papers are silent on the inner states they collect. No system expresses all seven dimensions strongly, and only 20 meet the definition. Slow and experience centered design comes closest, whereas persuasive technology and human-AI interaction score lowest. Factor and latent class analyses reveal two cultures of reflection, one working through form and the other through scaffolded thought, which only one system combines. Systems that let people set the pace score markedly higher, even with paradigm and form controlled (odds ratio 13.5). Hence, reflective computing is proposed as a paradigm whose aim is a human capacity rather than a system function, and which treats slowness as valuable only when people choose it.

Governments are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to deliver services, process cases and inform policy, but the success of these initiatives depends less on the technology than on the capabilities of the public workforce that must use, oversee and explain it. Evidence on how AI reshapes tasks suggests that routine cognitive work is most exposed, while demand grows for analytical, interpersonal and ethical judgement. Yet research on public-sector AI has concentrated on technology adoption and governance, and far less on the reskilling and leadership needed to make adoption work. This paper addresses that gap through an integrative review of literature from public administration, labour economics, leadership and learning science, supplemented by policy sources. The review identifies three capability clusters that AI-enabled public administration requires: digital-technical capability, human-relational capability and adaptive leadership capability. It also finds that evidence-based learning designs, particularly spaced, retrieval-based microlearning embedded in work, offer a scalable route to building these capabilities across large civil services. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and transformational leadership theory, the paper proposes the AI-Ready Public Workforce Capability Framework, which links institutional enablers, capability clusters and learning architecture to public value outcomes. Four propositions and practical recommendations are offered for public managers and training institutions, with reference to India’s Mission Karmayogi.

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools become increasingly integrated into higher education, understanding how engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity and responsible AI use has become increasingly important. OBJECTIVES: This study investigates how master’s engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity, and responsible AI use. It also explores the potential relevance of these practices for the development of competencies associated with participation in data-driven and AI-enabled professional environments. METHODS: A mixed-methods approach was employed using the PEDRA questionnaire (Perceptions on Ethics and Development of Responsibility in Academia), developed by the authors. The instrument was designed to explore students’ perceptions, experiences, and ethical reasoning regarding academic integrity and responsible research practices. The analysis focused on two questionnaire items addressing the influence of academic honesty on data use and the frequency of AI tool use in academic activities. The study involved master’s engineering students from two higher education institutions. RESULTS: Based on the 48 complete responses analysed, the findings indicate awareness of data integrity principles, particularly regarding anonymity, confidentiality, informed consent, and rigorous data analysis. Ethical referencing and transparency in data handling were mentioned less frequently, suggesting areas for further educational support. Regarding AI adoption, 21 of 48 respondents (43.8%) reported occasional use of AI tools, reflecting a cautious and exploratory approach. Descriptive differences in AI use were observed across age and gender groups, with female respondents being more likely to explore AI while maintaining ethical awareness, although these findings should be interpreted with caution. CONCLUSION: The study highlights the importance of integrating responsible data and AI practices into engineering education. The results suggest that developing students’ capacity to use data and AI critically, transparently, and ethically may support the development of competencies associated with responsible participation in increasingly digital and AI-enabled environments. The PEDRA questionnaire demonstrates potential as an exploratory and diagnostic instrument for identifying educational needs related to academic integrity, responsible AI use, data integrity, and trustworthy digital practice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Across biology, artificial intelligence and social systems, interacting components develop specialised functions and collective capabilities that were not individually specified in advance. Examples range from reorganised living cells to functionally differentiated neural networks and collective decisions in animal groups. What organisational principles might account for these outcomes—and for consciousness?We propose the Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) Hypothesis. Within physical and environmental constraints, causally accessible, information-mediated interactions among changeable components can generate organisational structures that alter subsequent interactions and enable new functions. SOIPS distinguishes a generative engine from Dimension A, describing informational organisation from functional signalling to context-sensitive coordination, and Dimension B, comprising the elementary functional families of retention, inference and regulation. Particular configurations of these elements support composite capabilities, including perception, memory, learning, agency and cognition. Developed capabilities can reshape their own organisational conditions, combine with other functions and contribute to systems at new organisational scales.Within this framework, consciousness is proposed as a configuration in which awareness-related information participates in flexible cognition. Awareness refers to the organised availability of information about relevant internal or external conditions. Consciousness is thus neither an inevitable endpoint of increasing complexity nor a capability restricted by definition to human biology. If experience is constituted by particular organised neural activity, SOIPS may also help investigate the origins of phenomenal experience.SOIPS offers a shared language for interpreting biological development, learned organisation in AI and collective behaviour. It also motivates testable predictions: changing information access, constraints or elementary functional contributions should alter the capabilities they support. Cross-domain interventions could assess whether analogous organisational relationships produce comparable outcomes, informing both scientific explanation and the design of artificial agents and institutions.

documents.abstract: The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into educational feedback offers opportunities to expand personalisation and accessibility, but it also raises risks of bias, opacity and the erosion of teacher mediation. The objective of this theoretical-conceptual article was to propose a framework to guide the use of generative AI in feedback from the standpoint of inclusive assessment and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). As method, a selective narrative review of the literature on inclusive assessment, formative feedback and AI in education was conducted across three strands, which were then integrated into a framework of teacher decisions and transversal criteria, contrasted with related models and complemented by a focused search of recent studies on trust and evaluative judgement. As a result, the framework links four teacher decisions (what is assessed, how evidence is gathered, how feedback is given, and what opportunities for improvement are offered) with three transversal quality criteria: accessibility, agency and dialogue, and equity with data protection. It is complemented by a four-level scale of teacher mediation that distinguishes lower- and higher-risk uses, a checklist for reviewing AI-supported feedback before it reaches students, three illustrative examples, and five testable propositions to guide empirical validation. The implications of the framework for teaching practice and institutional policy are discussed, along with its tensions (efficiency versus dialogicity, personalisation versus privacy, linguistic diversity, and the access gap) and its methodological limitations. The article concludes that inclusion does not depend on the tool but on the pedagogical and ethical decisions that govern its use, and that teacher responsibility for interpreting evidence remains irreplaceable.

AI systems are increasingly present in children's everyday environments: education, entertainment, social networks, and toys. Their safety is typically assessed at the model level, through benchmarks, red-teaming, and content filtering. However, most AI harm taxonomies lack child-specific evidence and under-specify developmental harm and the stakeholder asymmetries unique to minors. Building on prior taxonomies, we construct a child-centered harm taxonomy mapped to sociotechnical failure modes. We curate and code 1331 publicly reported child-related AI incidents, annotating internal and external harm types and the failure mode implicated in each incident. Our analysis reveals which harms are most prevalent in public reporting, how individual-level and population-level harms relate, and which failures are most often coded alongside harm. We find that harm concentrates in representational, dignity-related, and psychological categories, and co-occurs most often with deployment-context, governance, and misuse failures rather than model defects. Harm to an individual child is also frequently linked to population-level harm, reaching children who never interacted with the system. These findings suggest that model-level evaluations, while necessary, cannot by themselves anticipate the harm pathways most often documented for children. We conclude with actionable implications emphasizing mitigations beyond model-level safeguards such as content filtering: age assurance, consent verification for depiction, safety-by-design UX constraints, incident disclosure norms, and auditing regimes targeting developmental risk. Privacy-minimized annotations, a codebook, and documentation are available at https://github.com/The-Responsible-AI-Initiative/KidAID.

documents.abstract: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.

Cybersecurity is increasingly recognised as a complex adaptive socio-technical system in which security outcomes emerge from the interactions of attackers, defenders, users, organisations, regulators, and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents. These interactions generate adaptive feedback loops, strategic behaviour, information diffusion, and network effects that drive the evolution of cyber threats and defences. Consequently, phenomena such as attack propagation, cyber-risk contagion, cascading failures, and systemic resilience cannot be fully understood through static or purely technical perspectives. Although evolutionary game theory (EGT), complex systems science, network science, behavioural research, and cyber economics have each provided valuable insights, the literature remains fragmented, with no unified perspective for explaining cybersecurity as an evolving socio-technical ecosystem. This review develops the concept of Social Physics of Cybersecurity as an interdisciplinary perspective that brings these approaches together with human-AI interaction to explain how collective security outcomes emerge from adaptive interactions within interconnected cyber ecosystems. We synthesise research on attacker-defender co-evolution, finite and structured population dynamics, cyber contagion, critical transitions, systemic cyber risk, and the growing role of AI-enabled multi-agent systems. Building on these perspectives, we propose a unified multilevel view of cybersecurity that links individual strategic behaviour, network-level interactions, and system-wide resilience. We argue that cybersecurity should be understood as a social-physical phenomenon in which resilience and vulnerability emerge from the collective dynamics of interacting human and artificial agents. Finally, we identify key research opportunities for developing empirically grounded, data-driven, and AI-enabled models capable of predicting, analysing, and governing increasingly interconnected and autonomous cyber ecosystems.

Individuals with intellectual disabilities face entrenched systemic and cultural barriers to sexual expression, often exacerbated in Chinese contexts by values of ‘face’ and ‘familism’. While artificial intelligence and humanoid sex robots emerge as potential interventions, their ethical and practical viability within disability services remains contested. This study employed Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the perspectives of 12 Chinese social workers regarding the integration of AI-powered intimate technologies. Findings reveal four major themes: systemic barriers to romantic agency, the perceived benefits of ‘risk-free’ simulated intimacy, ethical concerns regarding relational authenticity, and societal reflections on the ‘eternal child’ syndrome. Practitioners recognised robots as tools to bypass parental opposition and institutional liability by eliminating risks of pregnancy and exploitation. However, a critical tension emerged: whether these technologies genuinely empower users or serve as a ‘techno-fix’ to hide disabled sexuality from the neurotypical public. The results highlight a ‘double standard of readiness’, where cognitive competence is used to gatekeep human rights. We argue for a multidisciplinary governance framework that prioritises ‘techno-social’ literacy and challenges the sexual ableism inherent in current service models.

documents.abstract: Sovereign artificial intelligence has moved from a legal debate about data residency to a practical question of agency across the whole computational value chain: energy, connectivity, data centres, compute, data, models, applications, skills and governance. This paper reviews an AI-generated report that models national compute ecosystems through infrastructure economics, low-precision arithmetic, game theory and Monte Carlo risk analysis, and augments it into a verified academic treatment. Each empirical claim in the source was checked against institutional sources. Several were confirmed: the scale of the CNAS Sovereign AI Index, the UK Council for Science and Technology's definition of sovereignty as agency, the European AI Gigafactories call and its deadline changes, Bangladesh's draft National AI Policy 2026–2030, the OECD's 2026 due diligence guidance and the specifications of current rack-scale systems. Others were corrected, notably the infrastructure share of projects and the temporary nature of a mid-2026 suspension of foreign access to frontier models; unverifiable figures were removed. The augmentation adds three computed analyses. A synthetic quantisation experiment shows why block-scaled 4-bit formats are central to doing more with scarce national compute. A corrected analysis of the source's openness model shows that its optimum is a single planner's choice, not a Nash equilibrium, and derives its comparative statics. A Monte Carlo schedule model shows that headline probabilities of infrastructure delay depend entirely on assumed distributions and should be reported with them. The paper closes with implications for capital-constrained states, with Bangladesh as a reference case, framed at the level of strategy and policy.

Objective To investigate the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) readiness among nursing students and analyze its influencing factors, providing evidence for the cultivation of AI literacy in nursing education. Methods A total of 684 nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province were recruited as study participants. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire and the Chinese version of the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (C-MAIRS-MS). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were employed for data processing. Results The overall mean score of AI readiness among nursing students was 3.47 ± 0.31; the cognitive dimension scored the highest (3.57 ± 0.44), while the competency dimension scored the lowest (3.32 ± 0.48). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that education level, Self-rated academic performance, Student cadre, Innovation and entrepreneurship project, Large language model use frequency, AI course learning, Programming foundation were significant predictors of AI readiness, collectively explaining 33.3% of the total variance (R 2 = 0.333, adjusted R 2 = 0.311, F = 15.030, P < 0.001) Conclusion Nursing students’ AI readiness remains suboptimal with room for improvement. Targeted interventions addressing key predictors are essential to strengthen AI competency among nursing students.

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support independent preparation without necessarily strengthening students’ connections to the classroom. We examined a structured instructional protocol combining AI exploration, confidence reflection, unresolved question generation, and instructor responsiveness. Following baseline assessment, six intact undergraduate class sections at one Chinese university were randomized equally, with three sections and 110 students assigned to each condition. Assessments were conducted in Weeks 1, 6, and 12, and the intervention began in Week 2. Recomputed item means were analyzed using equally weighted section-level contrasts with four degrees of freedom, supplemented by exact randomization tests. At Week 12, the between-condition difference in classroom belonging change was 0.361 (95% CI 0.145 to 0.576; Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.029). The corresponding differences were 0.282 for emotional engagement, − 0.497 for reactance to teacher guidance, and − 15.24 points for the confidence–performance discrepancy index (CPDI). Exact two-sided randomization p values were 0.100 for all primary contrasts, the minimum attainable with six balanced sections. Exploratory individual-level pathway and effect-modification analyses were treated as hypothesis-generating because only six sections were observed and the pathway estimates were sensitive to measurement timing. Overall, the structured protocol showed promising differences in classroom belonging and related outcomes, but inference remains limited by the small number of randomized sections, parametric model assumptions, and the preliminary discrepancy measure. The findings therefore concern the combined instructional protocol rather than an isolated effect of GenAI or an established psychological mechanism.

Abstract Graduate employability programmes are usually evaluated with self-report measures. We compared a structured human resource development programme supported by generative AI with career guidance matched on topics, duration and facilitator contact. Twelve intact cohorts of graduates seeking education-sector posts in Guangdong, China (N = 186), were allocated as whole units, six per condition, crossed with institution, facilitator and schedule. Blinded experts gave a global rating (0–100) of recruitment-task materials produced on site, under invigilation and without AI, before and after the programme. Ratings were made without a pre-specified rubric, which limits their interpretation. Among 168 participants with post-test data (overall attrition 9.7%), the adjusted difference favoured the AI-supported programme by 5.38 points (95% CI 2.76 to 8.01; d = 0.60) and was stable across eight specifications. Four new self-report scales showed smaller differences (d = 0.12 to 0.29), none significant after Holm correction; each scale could detect only differences of about d = 0.4. The effect on expert ratings exceeded the mean effect on self-report by 0.37 standard deviations (95% CI 0.10 to 0.63). Component analyses were exploratory. The design cannot separate the contribution of AI from structured practice and feedback.

documents.abstract: This paper investigates how situated AI literacy is conceptualised and enacted in complex and heterogeneous ed­ucational environments such as Adult Education Centres in Italy. Qualitative data from semi-structured inter­views with ten headmasters and open-ended responses from forty-five teachers to an online questionnaire were thematically analysed. The findings suggest that headmasters advocate for more than mere technical training, articulating context-sensitive and practice-oriented views of teachers’ professional development in AI literacy. Teachers’ descriptions of their interactions with GenAI illustrate practices of evaluating, adjusting, and modi­fying AI-generated content, suggesting that the development of AI literacy occurs through practices of repair and maintenance in artificial conversations. Therefore, this study suggests participatory action research as a valuable approach for teachers’ professional development in AI literacy to account for their practices while providing them with space and time for critical reflection and practical experimentation with Generative AI in superdiverse educational environments.

Abstract An institutional artificial intelligence (AI) agent may encounter an instruction to issue a refund inside a petition it was asked to summarise. The same tool call may be legitimate when requested by an officer and unauthorised when induced by that petition. We address this distinction with teleoneutrosophic values, pairing separate neutrosophic triples for effect and purpose. A provenance discount and evidence fusion feed a guard that authorises, escalates or denies a proposed call. We characterise paraconsistency and adjunction in the induced matrix logic and prove conditional limits on untrusted influence. With reliable labels and call attribution, a source cannot supply purpose support above its trust cap, and untrusted evidence cannot justify denial. Tests on 1,054 InjecAgent attack cases and synthetic e-government scenarios show where grading helps and where crisp protection suffices. On low-trust channels, the guard can reduce to taint-and-escalate; an attribution-based plan/data rule is at least as safe. Retaining ambivalence about an unrequested call reduces worst-case direct-harm pass-through after channel mislabelling from 100\% to 34.5\% on InjecAgent and 25.0\% on the synthetic benchmark. A learned estimator that omits the trust label reduces direct-harm pass-through under ordinary mislabelling from 36.7\% to 1.6\%. The results identify a role for independent ambivalence in provenance-aware authorisation and expose the limits on automation when legitimate external requests are missing from training data.

Code, materials and derived data for the preprint “The analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis: a framework, open tools, and a screening study” (van Allen, 2026). In the screening study, two large language models coded 40 open-access smoking-cessation trial reports for 94 behaviour change techniques under a half-fraction factorial design (32 configurations, 38 runs). Every run was scored against Human Behaviour-Change Project annotations. The project contains the prospective multiverse declaration, the prompts and codebook, the report × code decisions of every run, the reference, the figures, and analysis scripts that reproduce every reported result without new model calls. No report text or quotations are included. The tools and declaration can be adapted to run comparable multiverse studies on other data.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the accounting profession by automating routine tasks, improving data accuracy, and enabling more strategic decision-making. This paper, titled The Blessed Accountant: How Artificial Intelligence Reclaims Time, Eliminates Error, and Elevates Strategy, examines the evolving role of AI in modern accounting and its implications for accounting professionals, organizations, and financial management. AI-powered tools can streamline bookkeeping, invoice processing, bank reconciliations, tax compliance, fraud detection, and financial reporting, thereby reducing manual workloads and minimizing the risk of human error. Beyond operational efficiency, AI enables accountants to shift their focus from repetitive transactional activities toward analytical interpretation, strategic planning, risk management, and advisory services. The paper also explores the challenges associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, technological dependence, and the need for continuous professional development. It emphasizes that AI should be viewed not as a replacement for accountants but as an enabling technology that strengthens professional judgment, ethical responsibility, and value creation. The effective integration of AI into accounting requires a balanced approach that combines technological innovation with human expertise, regulatory compliance, and appropriate governance mechanisms. The study concludes that AI has the potential to redefine accounting as a more efficient, accurate, and strategically oriented profession, provided that its adoption is guided by transparency, accountability, and responsible use. Ultimately, the future of accounting lies in the collaboration between intelligent technologies and skilled professionals, empowering accountants to deliver greater organizational value.

Background: Negative life events are associated with lower well-being in children, and this association may vary with physical activity and motivational quality. Objectives: This study examined gender differences in negative life events, physical activity, motivation, and well-being and tested whether moderate and vigorous physical activity moderated the association between negative life events and well-being. It further explored whether intrinsic motivation extended this moderating relationship. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 752 children aged 8–14 years (335 boys, 417 girls; mean = 10.36 years) and their parents. Parents reported negative life events and physical activity; children reported well-being and intrinsic motivation. Moderation analyses were conducted separately by gender, alongside formal tests of gender differences. Results: Parents rated negative life events more severe for girls. Girls also reported lower vigorous physical activity, intrinsic motivation, and well-being. Greater event severity was associated with lower well-being in boys and girls. Formal gender differences in moderations were significant for vigorous but not for moderate physical activity. Follow-up gender-stratified analyses showed that, among girls, higher moderate activity was associated with a weaker negative association between event severity and well-being, whereas higher vigorous activity was associated with a stronger negative association. No interactions were observed among boys. The three-way interactions involving intrinsic motivation were non-significant. Conclusion: A statistically significant difference in moderations was observed for vigorous but not for moderate physical activity. Thus, gender-stratified findings for moderate activity should be considered exploratory. Given the cross-sectional design and subjective assessment of physical activity intensity, findings should be interpreted as associative.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being adopted in tourism and hospitality education more quickly than the pedagogical guidance needed to use it well. This study developed the GATE Framework, a GenAI-enhanced active learning environment intended to develop tourism communication competency, and examined its appropriateness through expert review. The work comprised two stages within the first research phase. An evidence-informed synthesis established three connected layers: Inputs, Core Process Components, and Outcomes. At the center of the Process Layer is an iterative Explore-Generate-Apply-Reflect cycle, supported by human-AI interaction, authentic tourism tasks, peer and instructor participation, reflection, and adaptive feedback. In the second stage, nine experts in tourism and hospitality, curriculum and instruction, educational technology, AI in education, and active learning then evaluated the framework using an 18-item, five-point scale and four open-ended questions. The overall rating was very high (x̄ = 4.54, S.D. = 0.58), and the five domain means ranged from 4.52 to 4.56. The experts gave their strongest ratings to the framework's theoretical alignment, relevance to tourism communication learning, and suitability for further development. Ratings remained favorable but were lower for the definition of individual roles and the practical sequence of the learning process. In response, the framework was revised to clarify scaffolding and human oversight, strengthen privacy and transparency provisions, and give greater weight to tourism content rooted in local culture. The resulting framework provides the conceptual basis for GATE-SLE, where GenAI assists disciplinary learning without displacing human judgment.

This essay argues that a person who teaches an AI agent their way of working, one correction at a time, builds a copy of themselves, and that whether the copy replaces them or works for them depends on who owns it. Drawing on eight months of the author's own logs, it separates knowledge, which moves into the machine and gets cheaper, from judgment, which decides the next rule the machine needs. It describes a "higher self", a copy that remembers the rules its owner forgets and can argue against them with their own reasons, and the opposite risk of delegating decisions to an agent that has learned nothing from its user. It answers the objection that such teaching trains a replacement, with reference to Taylor, Braverman, Amodei and Altman, and proposes that a person's way of working, written down as rules, should belong to them and travel with them between employers, while the processes, data and clients of a company stay with the company.

documents.abstract: Education 6.0 has emerged as a conceptual orientation through which scholars explore the future of education in contexts shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), adaptive learning, human–machine collaboration, epistemic pluralism, and complex societal transformation. Yet the growing use of the label raises important questions concerning its intellectual genealogy, conceptual coherence, and relationship to earlier educational paradigms. This critical review examines selected publications from 2023 to 2026 to reconstruct the documented development of Education 6.0, distinguish its principal conceptual strands, and identify directions for theoretical and empirical research. Particular attention is given to Pitshou Moleka’s 2023 publications, including Dispelling the Limitations of Education 5.0 and Outlining the Vision of Education 6.0 and Exploring the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Education 6.0: Enhancing Personalized Learning and Adaptive Pedagogy. The review also considers subsequent contributions addressing AI-enabled personalization, human-centred educational technology, interdisciplinary learning, cultural knowledge, and ethical governance. It argues that Education 6.0 should not be treated as a universally standardized model but as an emerging and internally differentiated conceptual field. The review proposes a five-dimensional analytical framework encompassing pedagogical adaptability, human agency, ethical governance, epistemic pluralism, and systemic sustainability. This framework offers a basis for comparing competing formulations and designing empirical studies. The review identifies Moleka’s 2023 publications as documented early contributions to the conceptual development of Education 6.0, while recognizing that establishing exclusive intellectual priority would require a broader and reproducible examination of antecedent literature.

Algorithmic fairness is commonly evaluated among people who have already reached an automated decision. Yet an institution may shape who reaches that decision by announcing AI screening, imposing digital prerequisites, presenting discouraging eligibility signals, or requiring complex machine-mediated interactions. People who do not apply may leave no decision record, no appeal, and no trace in conventional fairness dashboards. This conceptual study develops the Invisible Denominator Framework (IDF), which distinguishes decision-stage disparity from participation-stage exclusion and identifies five mechanisms through which algorithmic environments can alter entry into opportunity systems. Through a structured, non-systematic synthesis of administrative-burden theory, applicant-reaction experiments, sociotechnical fairness, selective-label research, and institutional AI governance, the paper specifies the boundary conditions under which non-participation should be treated as a potential equity concern rather than automatically as discrimination. It develops seven testable propositions, an upstream access assurance protocol, and a comparative empirical agenda for recruitment, social protection, education, and credit. The central contribution is a change in the unit of fairness assessment: from outcomes conditional on application to the opportunities, costs, perceptions, and constraints shaping who can apply. Because the population of deterred non-applicants is partly unobserved, the framework recommends triangulation, sensitivity analysis, privacy-preserving outreach, and explicit reporting of uncertainty rather than an unsupported single fairness score. The analysis offers a practical route to making participation-stage harms visible without conflating all non-participation with wrongful exclusion.

documents.abstract: The knowledge acquisition bottleneck was the greatest obstacle of the second AI boom: expert systems could reason with rules, but extracting those rules from human experts proved extraordinarily difficult. This essay revisits CA Outlook, an expert system the author developed at IBM Japan in the late 1980s to forecast hardware revenue, and asks what has become of the bottleneck in the age of large language models (LLMs). By learning from vast amounts of text, LLMs appear to have cleared the wall of knowledge acquisition. Yet organization-specific tacit knowledge, the judgment of when to trust model output, and the redesign of work all remain on the organization's side. The bottleneck has not disappeared; it has moved to organizational capability, as the IT–organizational capability dependency theory predicts. The CA Outlook experience also shows that management trusted explainable multiple regression over an opaque AI, a lesson that applies to today's black-box models. Finally, the essay argues that two features of Japanese management, multi-skilling through job rotation and long-term employment, produce people who can supervise chains of AI agents and workplaces where employees have no reason to withhold know-how from AI, giving Japan a real but time-limited opportunity.

Limited research has examined the decision-making process of officers during potentially volatile interactions with the public. To provide an initial understanding of this process in Canada, we conducted interviews using the Critical Decision Method with 23 Winnipeg Police officers with a variety of experiences (e.g. junior members, tactical officers). Using grounded theory methodology, we developed a theory that explains an officer’s decision-making process during potential use-of-force incidents. Our theory, the process of preserving life, has two main components: (1) the decision-making process involved in preserving life; and (2) the overarching factors that influence officer decision-making. We found that officers have expertise in responding to potential use-of-force incidents and that tactical officers have some unique elements of enhanced decision-making. Based on our findings, we discuss implications for officer training and future research.

This commentary highlights the age illusion and advocates integrating biological age and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance clinical precision in health care. By synthesizing geroscience and machine learning, practitioners and scientists can effectively bridge the gap between experimental biomarkers and personalized medicine and longevity care. This contribution is timely as the importance of biological age and predictive analytics offer transformative potential for diagnostics while necessitating a focus on modern medical systems. This article aims to elucidate how AI accelerates the clinical implementation of biological age rather than current chronological age in precision medicine.

documents.abstract: Purpose of Review Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the tasks performed by physicians, raising questions about how graduate medical education should prepare trainees for future practice and whether residency workforce planning should change as AI adoption expands. This brief review examines the implications of AI for residency education and physician workforce planning, using radiology as an early model of technology-driven task transformation while considering broader effects across diagnostic, procedural, and relationship-based specialties. Recent Findings AI is already being used for clinical documentation, image interpretation, predictive analytics, administrative workflows, and large-scale data analysis. AI-assisted scribing has particular relevance to chronic pain and other documentation-intensive specialties, where it may reduce clerical burden and preserve clinician attention for patient care. However, current evidence more strongly supports task redistribution and physician augmentation than complete replacement. Specialties built around standardized digital information may experience earlier automation, whereas procedural skill, complex communication, longitudinal judgment, and responsibility for final clinical decisions remain difficult to substitute. At present, broad reductions in residency positions based only on anticipated AI capabilities seem premature. Summary Residency programs should adapt curricula now by incorporating AI literacy, verification skills, data interpretation, and safeguards against deskilling. Changes in residency position numbers should occur more cautiously and should be based on durable, specialty-specific workforce evidence, including hiring patterns, patient access, workload, productivity, and regional need. The goal should be to train physicians who can safely supervise and integrate AI while preserving the human expertise that remains central to high-quality care.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in daily life, ascertaining whether an agent is human is critical. Here we systematically benchmark AI's ability to imitate humans in three language tasks (image captioning, word association and conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection and attention prediction), collecting data from n = 636 humans and 37 AI agents. We also conducted 72,191 Turing-like tests with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges. Current AIs are approaching the ability to convincingly impersonate humans and deceive human judges in both language and vision. Even simple AI judges outperformed humans in distinguishing AI from human responses. Imitation ability showed minimal correlation with conventional AI performance metrics, suggesting that passing as human is an important independent evaluation criterion. The large-scale Turing-like datasets and metrics introduced here offer valuable benchmarks for assessing human-likeness in AI and highlight the importance of rigorous, quantitative imitation tests for AI development.

documents.abstract: Perceived safety in public spaces is shaped by emotional, cognitive, social, and environmental factors, presenting a complex HCI design challenge. This study examines how women’s perceived safety varies across environmental contexts and how these experiences can inform context-aware smart wearable garments. A pilot study (n = 20) refined a 31-item questionnaire, followed by a main study of 199 valid respondents. A two-way ANOVA identified significant main effects of Gender and Living Environment on safety concern, with women reporting greater concern than men across Urban, Intra-urban, and Rural settings. PCA identified one dominant environmental-safety component containing three descriptive design factors: fear of physical harm, environmental discomfort, and socially situated risk. A second PCA identified Proactive Personal Safety and Environmental Awareness as priority smart-garment domains. These findings informed three design models and a proof-of-concept prototype linking user perception, environmental sensing, and adaptive feedback.

The swift progression of digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the educational landscape, creating both challenges and opportunities for asynchronous IT-related courses in public administration (PA) programs. For future public servants, such courses are not only vehicles for content delivery, but also spaces in which foundational competencies such as digital literacy, problem-solving, autonomous learning, and the effective use of technology in administrative contexts can be strengthened. This article outlines a framework for improving professor–student interaction and asynchronous course delivery, drawing on institutional research and relevant e-learning literature. It reports the outcomes of a university research project aimed at personalizing learning experiences through visual technologies, gamification, and AI-supported assistance, with particular attention to one introductory computer science course. The article presents an exploratory comparison of three naturally occurring cohorts of students in three consecutive academic years, examining how the staged integration of gamification and a GPT-4–based assistant coincided with changes in academic performance. The results show performance improvements across cohorts exposed to increasingly innovative delivery approaches. In a quasi-experimental comparison, exam performance improved following the staged introduction of gamification and AI-supported assistance, while the findings also suggest the broader pedagogical relevance of such tools for preparing PA students for digitally mediated professional environments.

Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.

The growing use of intelligence in legal research has opened new chances for speed yet it has also sparked worries about how accurate and trustworthy legal authorities are. These worries were highlighted in the case of Pooja Ramesh Singh versus Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. In that case the Supreme Court of India looked at how the National Company Law Tribunal had used fabricated and artificial intelligence‑generated material. The core dispute was about enforcing a guarantee but the Supreme Court's ruling brought up a wider issue: how can courts stay honest if they rely on fake authorities as legal precedent? This paper looks at the facts of the case the Supreme Court's reasoning and what it means for lawyers, judges and the whole legal field. It points out the line between using artificial intelligence as a research helper and treating artificial intelligence output as an official source of law. The paper also talks about the duty of lawyers to check citations. The need for courts and tribunals to verify the authenticity of the authorities they see. Even though artificial intelligence can make research faster this paper says that convenience cannot replace careful work or judicial responsibility. The Supreme Court's decision reaffirms that legal choices must be based on trustworthy sources of law. It also asks questions about fair disciplinary actions and the safeguards that are needed as artificial intelligence grows in law practice. In the end this paper says that while technology can help thinking the responsibility, for the correctness and honesty of legal papers must stay with human professionals.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely discussed in higher education in relation to learning, assessment design, and academic integrity. Much of this discussion, however, treats students’ AI use as a set of discrete academic practices, rather than as part of broader decision-making that spans learning and everyday life. This piece argues that students’ academic and non-academic uses of AI increasingly shape one another, influencing how they approach uncertainty, manage emotional pressure, and make judgements when learning feels high stakes. Drawing on academic advising and personal tutoring conversations, it shows that students are not using AI solely to generate outputs, but to talk ideas through, test interpretations, and steady their thinking when confidence and academic identity are in play. These practices closely resemble the relational and cognitive work advisers already support and make visible how AI is now being used to sustain the emotional work of learning that underpins sound judgement. A practice-based framework is presented describing four overlapping modes of student AI use - instrumental, dialogic, metacognitive, and affective-regulatory - each aligned with established advising functions. Rather than positioning AI as a threat to academic integrity or professional judgement, the paper argues for advising as guidance: supporting students to recognise how AI shapes their thinking, to develop appropriate boundaries, and to make learning decisions with confidence and responsibility.

documents.abstract: Generative AI can produce code, tests, documentation, and technical explanations that resemble artefacts traditionally used as evidence of student competence, weakening the inference from artefact quality to the engineering capability behind it. We report the redesign and first deployment of a 13-week, AI-permissive, software-intensive engineering course in which students may delegate substantial work to AI while retaining responsibility for planning, verification, review, integration, and explanation. The redesign couples an engineering accountability workflow, which structures human-AI work and preserves human decision authority, with an assessment evidence architecture comprising six complementary channels: product, process/origin, verification, explanation, reflection, and individual assurance. A collect--cross-check--escalate (CCE) reasoning logic connects these channels rather than treating any single artefact or trace as sufficient evidence of competence. By the end of Week 11, the deployment involved 87 students organised into 17 teams, with 957 individual weekly Git repositories and 34 group-project Git repositories supporting repeated assessment and engineering activity. The first deployment yielded four practical lessons: AI assistance changes where rubric criteria carry evidential weight; multiple evidence channels require deliberate cross-checking and meaningful complementarity; the evidential strength realised in practice may differ from that intended in the assessment design; and automation scales evidence collection more readily than interpretation. The contribution is a conceptually grounded, deployed design for making engineering responsibility and competence more visible when AI can perform substantial artefact production.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents can synthesise scientific arguments and construct computational models rapidly, but fluency is not scientific validity. Neither expert status, human oversight, multi-agent consensus, publication nor patent protection substitutes for independent empirical testing. Experiments themselves can conflict because of bias, measurement error or genuine biological heterogeneity. We propose an evidence-to-decision trust architecture for drug research and model-informed drug development (MIDD) that links verifiable primary observations, provenance and uncertainty to competing mechanistic hypotheses, adversarial AI review, discriminating experiments and accountable decisions. Credibility is evaluated for a specified context of use, not assigned globally to people or algorithms. The framework spans target validation, translational pharmacology, dosing, clinical development and regulatory assessment, illustrated by a proposed IQANOVA ATLAS AI–quantitative systems pharmacology (AI-QSP) workflow. We extend the framework to regulatory agencies using AI agents: scientific assessment and model credibility are distinct from the legally binding act of medicine authorisation. Inspired by Juvenal's question of who checks the guardians and the historical Rabkrin inspection debate, we propose auditable agent roles, explicit legal decision rights, independent scrutiny and routes for challenge. A synthetic SBML/SED-ML/COMBINE package with provenance ontologies illustrates reproducible reporting without claiming biological validation. A prospective benchmark is proposed to test scientific quality, regulatory decision loss, agent independence and appeal outcomes. The final question—whether, when and under whose authority an AI could make binding decisions—remains unresolved.

documents.abstract: This academic article aims to 1) synthesize concepts and theories explaining sustainable school administration in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), 2) analyze the opportunities and risks of AI in each domain of school administration, and 3) propose a model and recommendations for school administrators and policymakers. The author conducted an integrative literature review and qualitative document analysis of 44 documents, organized by Thailand's four domains of school administration (academic affairs, personnel, budget, and general administration), using sustainable leadership, sociotechnical systems theory, and TPACK as analytical lenses. The synthesis shows that AI can support personalized learning, reduce teachers' non-teaching workload, and strengthen data-informed decisions. However, school-based evidence remains limited, and AI use carries risks of privacy breaches, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, and long-term costs. The article proposes the SAISA Model (Sustainable AI-Integrated School Administration), comprising inputs, four administrative processes anchored by data governance, outputs, sustainability outcomes, and an assessment-and-learning feedback loop, with recommendations for school administrators, educational service area offices, and policymakers.
